body_markdown:
The[Fiat 124 Sport Spider](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1971-fiat-124-sport-spider/) is the most plentiful 20th-century Italian car in American car graveyards today, having held that crown for decades. This makes sense, given that it was sold here from 1967 through 1985 (including the ones badged as Pininfarina Azzurras) and owners tend to hang onto non-runners for decades. Its sedan big brother, however, is another story; today’s FPS subject is the first discarded example I’ve found in this country for at least 20 years.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This car currently resides at[a self-service yard just north of downtown Denver, Colorado](https://www.upullandpay.com/locations/colorado/denver/) .


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


Fiat offered an extensive lineup of cars in the United States during most of the 1970s, with sales of the company’s fuel-efficient machines surging once the geopolitical fallout of the 1973 Yom Kippur War resulted in[skyrocketing fuel prices](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1969-1976/oil-embargo) here. In mid-1974, when the magazine advertisement above was published, those 77¢–$1.80 gas prices were the equivalent of $5.29–$12.38 per gallon[in today’s money](https://murileemartin.substack.com/p/your-handy-inflationary-car-price) .


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


The[124 series](https://www.media.stellantis.com/em-en/heritage-hub-italy/press/mi-chiamo-fiat-124-at-the-heritage-hub-the-story-of-the-italian-saloon-that-conquered-the-world) first went on sale in the U.S. for the 1967 model year, as the successor to[the 1100](http://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/2014/03/junkyard-find-1963-fiat-1100d/) . That first year, it was available just in four-door sedan and station wagon forms. 124 sport coupes and convertibles followed soon after.


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


The temptingly cheap[128 subcompact](https://www.autoblog.com/news/junkyard-gem-1979-fiat-128-custom-sedan/) was Fiat’s biggest seller here during most of the early-to-middle 1970s, but fairly respectable numbers of non-Spider 124s hit American streets as well. Sales of the 124 sedan, wagon, and coupe continued here through the 1974 model year.


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


In Western Europe, the 124 was a huge sales success. Other than the Sport Spider, it was replaced there and in North America by the 131 (badged as[the Brava](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1980-fiat-brava/) on our shores) for 1975… but that was just the relatively short first chapter of the 124’s story.


Во́лжский автомоби́льный заво́д


The USSR’s Во́лжский автомоби́льный заво́д (Volga Automotive Plant) paid to license the 124’s design and began building a version in 1970 modified for harsh Soviet conditions. This was the VAZ-2101 Zhiguli, better known as the Lada on our side of the Iron Curtain.


Во́лжский автомоби́льный заво́д


The Lada was available in Western Europe and Canada, but not in the United States. The original VAZ-2101 was built in the Soviet Union through the late 1980s, but the Sovietized 124’s Siberia-hardened design was nowhere near done being useful by that point.


There were too many variations and direct descendants of the VAZ-2101 to list here. Those members of the extended 124 family were built until a decade-or-so ago, when the last VAZ-2017 Rivas were assembled by Suzuki in Egypt.


[Premier Automobiles Limited](https://driventowrite.com/2025/03/10/book-of-the-dead-premier/) built the European version of the 124 sedan (using the tooling from the[SEAT-built Spanish-market 124](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tcckd83f0Nw) ) in India from the middle 1980s through 2001. This car was badged as the 118NE; the final versions were built with Nissan engines, with assembly help from Peugeot.


All of this means that the Fiat 124 ranks up there with such legends as the Volkswagen Type 1 Beetle, the BMC Mini, the Morris Oxford/Hindustan Ambassador, and the Kia Pride in the list of car models built on essentially the same platform for the longest production runs. That’s around a half-century for the 124, still short of the Beetle’s record by 15 years or so but very impressive nonetheless.


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


Like[the Renault 5](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1982-renault-le-car-deluxe-3-door/) , the 124 was available in the United States but never approached European-market sales numbers.


Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino S.p.A.


The MSRPs were great for what you got. For 1973, American Fiat shoppers could buy a new 124 Special sedan for $2419, or about $18,469 after inflation. Other U.S.-market four-door sedans with similar price tags that year were the Plymouth Cricket ($2017), Toyota Corolla ($2231), Dodge Colt ($2259), Ford Maverick ($2297), AMC Hornet ($2343), Mazda 808 ($2350), Chevrolet Nova ($2407), Plymouth Valiant ($2417), Toyota Corona ($2436), Subaru DL ($2439), Renault 12 ($2495), Opel 1900 ($2610), Austin Marina ($2625), and Datsun 610 ($2706). Sadly, the final year for the four-door Datsun 510 here was 1972.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The Special was a more meaningful 124 designation in Europe at the time, where it came with a hotter engine and nicer features; in the USA, it was used on every 124 sedan from model years 1970–74.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Background established, let’s move from general 124 history to today’s FPS car. The latch mechanisms in all but one of the doors were fused solid, and I didn’t feel like huffing hantavirus-laden rodent nesting material to crawl inside and remove the driver’s door panel so I could free up the door and look at the build tag. The VIN tag on the dash tells us it’s a 1973 124 Special, and that’s good enough.


Google Maps


I found some 1990s registration paperwork inside the car, which gave me its address 30 years ago. Sure enough, a look at Google Street view shows that it sat in the front yard of a house in a Denver suburb going back about 20 years. You can watch the trees grow as this car settles into the soil and its paint fades.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


This looks like a car whose owner loved driving it enough to hang onto it after something broke, but in the end the time and cost of fixing it up must have been too daunting.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


I think it spent its entire career in Colorado.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


There’s no telling the actual mileage, but it’s at least 82,621.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


These were fun cars to drive by the standards of the era—very agile with a snarling exhaust note that made it feel quicker than it actually was. This 1.4-liter twin-cam engine was rated at 68 horsepower and 77.5 pound-feet, good enough for a flyweight 2115-pound sedan to get out of its own way.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The base transmission was a five-speed manual (the 124 wagon for ’73 came with a four-speed manual), with a three-speed automatic available as an option.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It appears to have begun life with the automatic, then received a manual transplant later on. With the glut of 124 Sport Spiders in junkyards going back to the middle 1970s, such a swap could have been accomplished easily and affordably.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The 1980s Sanyo AM/FM/cassette deck and 1997 registration paperwork indicate that this car was still getting the job done as it approached age 25. That means it outlasted most of its erstwhile competitors.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It has a set of aftermarket alloy wheels, which I believe were made by[O.Z. Racing](https://www.ozracing.com/) in the 1980s.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


There’s an Olson CB antenna of 1970s vintage on the decklid.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


While today’s FPS car is the first non-Spider 124 I’ve found in an American junkyard since I started this silly automotive journalism career in 2007, I *have* documented a couple of VAZ-2101 sedans in the автоморга (“auto morgues”) during[a trip to Bulgaria](https://www.theautopian.com/why-im-flying-to-junkyards-around-the-world-to-buy-the-most-useless-part-of-any-car/) a couple of years back. One was[this early-1970s model](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a63024098/lada-sedan-bulgarian-junkyard-treasure/) , while[the other was about a decade newer](https://www.thetruthaboutcars.com/cars/down-on-the-junkyard/junkyard-find-lada-1200s-44510455) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


These Warsaw Pact 124s are still plentiful in Bulgaria and Romania, and I documented some good survivors on that trip.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


[This one](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a63324925/vaz-2101-lada-spotted-on-bulgarian-street/) has been parking in this spot in Varna (quite close to[the amazing Soviet-car-heavy Retro Museum](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/varna-retro-museum-gallery/) ) since at least 2012.


Could a 1973 Corolla survive *this?*


Preferable to a horse.


Yes, the 124 was assembled in South Korea, where it benefited from filmstrip-style commercials.
